3: \section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
4: 
5: A contextual bandit must learn which action to take from the rewards of the
6: actions it has already tried. An upper confidence bound (UCB) policy balances
7: learning and reward by adding an uncertainty bonus to each predicted reward,
8: then choosing an action with a large resulting score. The bonus matters: a
9: policy that understates uncertainty can stop exploring too soon, while an
10: excessively large bonus can overwhelm differences in predicted rewards.
11: 
12: With a nonlinear predictor, retraining changes how the model represents past
13: observations. For example, a recommender may refit its reward predictor after
14: each interaction, then recompute the gradients of all previously recommended
15: items. Their recorded rewards stay the same, but the matrix built from their
16: gradients changes. A narrower width computed from that new matrix does not by
17: itself establish greater statistical certainty. This paper asks when such a
18: change of matrix preserves a confidence guarantee, and what that guarantee
19: costs in an implemented policy.
20: 
21: \paragraph{Why the old and new matrices need different justifications.}
22: The usual sequential confidence argument uses a feature for each observation
23: that was fixed before its reward was seen. We call the matrix that accumulates
24: those collection-time features the \emph{reference matrix}. Its stored features
25: stay fixed, even as the predictor continues to learn. The \emph{current matrix}
26: instead recomputes the gradients of the same past samples at today's model
27: parameters. We call this recomputation \emph{relinearization} or \emph{replay};
28: it does not collect new rewards.
29: 
30: The distinction is statistical, not merely computational. Once the model has
31: learned from past rewards, its recomputed features can depend on those rewards.
32: The usual confidence argument therefore does not automatically apply to the
33: current matrix. In notation, a sample collected at round $s$ contributes
34: $\bq_s(a_s)=\nabla_\theta\mu_{\btheta_s}(x_s,a_s)$ to the reference matrix,
35: but contributes $\nabla_\theta\mu_{\btheta_t}(x_s,a_s)$ when replayed at
36: round $t$. The reference matrix retains the predictable rank-one update used by the
37: standard self-normalized confidence argument; the replayed matrix need not.
38: 
39: Existing methods make different choices here. NeuralUCB and NeuralTS store
40: gradient features as observations arrive
41: \citep{zhou2020neural,zhang2021neural}. Neural tangent kernel (NTK) methods can keep
42: uncertainty features at initialization \citep{kassraie2022neural}, while
43: neural-linear methods use linear uncertainty in a learned last-layer
44: representation \citep{riquelme2018deep}. Fixed network linearizations and
45: post-hoc Laplace approximations offer related ways to measure predictive
46: uncertainty \citep{maddox2021fast,daxberger2021laplace}. We study the additional
47: obligations created by replaying the historical gradients at the current
48: parameter.
49: 
50: \paragraph{The central result: valid transport can still be unhelpful.}
51: \emph{Confidence transport} means using a justified comparison between the
52: reference and current matrices to convert a reference confidence band into a
53: score based on current curvature. A \emph{certificate} is a bound that makes
54: such a comparison valid. The \emph{width} is the geometric part of the
55: uncertainty bonus; a confidence radius scales it, and a separate term covers
56: model bias.
57: 
58: Direct reference scoring is already available. Transport is worth studying
59: because it exposes what a policy must establish if it chooses to score with
60: current curvature instead. It supplies no new observations or additional
61: statistical information. In fact, with the same history, center, radius and
62: bias, the certified transported width is at least the direct reference width.
63: An exact actionwise correction recovers that reference width
64: (\Cref{prop:reference-width-floor}). This comparison leaves the ordering of
65: adaptive regret open: different bonuses can change actions, which changes the
66: data on which subsequent decisions are based.
67: 
68: Our controlled study makes the cost concrete. The evaluated Hessian-transport
69: policy uses bounds on prediction Hessians to certify the change of matrix. It
70: has higher mean regret than every comparator in every condition. Its
71: recorded optimism checks pass, but its regret bounds are larger than a simple
72: deterministic cap. Thus a confidence construction can be valid under its
73: assumptions, conservative in its bound, and poor as a decision rule. These are
74: separate questions, and the paper examines each one.
75: 
76: \paragraph{What the analysis provides.}
77: The theory connects a statistical confidence band to the score the algorithm
78: actually uses. \Cref{fig:transport-interfaces} separates the reference matrix
79: $\bVbar_t$, the current matrix $\bV_t$, an applied operator $\Calg_t$ that may
80: approximate it, and the numerical width $\hat s_t(a)$ returned by a solver.
81: The matrices are symmetric positive definite (SPD), so their inverse quadratic
82: forms define widths. Each step needs its own bound, available before the
83: selected reward is observed.
84: 
85: \begin{figure}[t]
86:  \centering
87:  \input{figures/transport_conceptual_interfaces.tex}
88:  \caption{The steps between a statistical confidence band and an implemented
89:  score. A bound on changing the matrix, a bound on approximating it, and a
90:  bound on the solver's output serve different purposes. The formal conditions
91:  are in \Cref{asm:abstract-transport}. Every scored action needs an upper-valid
92:  numerical width; only the selected action needs the stated sharpness bound.
93:  Both conditions refer to the same widths used to choose that action.}
94:  \label{fig:transport-interfaces}
95: \end{figure}
96: 
97: The transported-UCB theorem combines these bounds and gives a regret guarantee
98: in terms of the reference matrix's accumulated information
99: (\Cref{thm:transported-ucb}). A two-sided matrix comparison is essential for
100: this guarantee: one direction preserves the upper confidence score, and the
101: other controls the width of the action actually chosen. We obtain such
102: comparisons from established Thompson--Finsler geometry
103: \citep{thompson1963certain,nussbaum1994finsler} and give computable certificates
104: using changes in model gradients (\Cref{lem:factor-spd-path,cor:hessian-path-new}).
105: The geometry and the UCB potential argument are established tools. The
106: contribution is to state and connect the distinct statistical and computational
107: obligations of scoring with replayed curvature.
108: 
109: For squared loss, we also construct the center of the confidence band. A ridge
110: correction based on collection-time features adjusts the current nonlinear
111: prediction. The confidence band around this \emph{corrected center} remains valid along any
112: predictable parameter path in the certified region, with supplied Taylor and
113: misspecification error bounds (\Cref{cor:corrected-center-new}). It does not
114: require the nonlinear optimizer to converge. The error bounds still have a
115: cost: persistent model mismatch can make regret guarantees linear or vacuous.
116: The finite-dimensional and near-linear consequences are given in
117: \Cref{cor:finite-d-rate-new,cor:global-near-linear-new}.
118: 
119: The scaled-tanh model permits a simpler comparison because its gradient
120: directions are fixed and only their weights change. Comparing those weights
121: gives a horizon-independent endpoint certificate and a tighter category-based
122: version (\Cref{cor:tanh-relative-weights}). This specialization does not cover
123: general rotating neural gradients.
124: 
125: \paragraph{What the experiments establish.}
126: The main study uses a 29-parameter scaled-tanh model with dense matrices and
127: direct Cholesky solves in float64 (\Cref{sec:transport-followup}). It compares
128: four policies in three prespecified conditions, with 50 paired seeds per
129: condition. All nine pointwise paired intervals favor the comparators over
130: Hessian transport. Transport inflation dominates Hessian's bound; the reference
131: policy's own-trajectory bounds also remain vacuous. All policies, including
132: the uncertified naive control, pass the recorded optimism diagnostics. These
133: floating-point checks neither certify numerical enclosures nor establish that
134: the correction was necessary in the observed runs.
135: 
136: The conditions change the reward task as well as curvature. The results
137: therefore describe this fixed teacher, model and shared prediction-based
138: optimizer selection; they do not isolate a causal effect of drift. Subsequent
139: analyses explain scores on recorded histories and assess tighter certificates
140: there. They do not run alternative adaptive policies. The original near-linear
141: audit is reported separately in \Cref{sec:transport-instantiation}; its bound
142: is dominated by the base component rather than transport inflation.
143: Approximate operators, conjugate-gradient performance and end-to-end
144: scalability are outside the empirical study.
145: 
146: \paragraph{Reading the paper.}
147: \Cref{sec:abstract-transport} starts with the exact-matrix case, then states the
148: general theorem. \Cref{sec:corrected-center} explains how the confidence center
149: is constructed. Readers interested primarily in the findings can continue to
150: \Cref{sec:transport-followup} and return to the certificate constructions when
151: needed. Proofs and the full experimental protocol are in the appendices.
